explanations.answer: So they won't be defiled before the Passover
explanations.explanation: That's the reason John gives. They stayed outside "…to avoid being defiled and unable to eat the Passover." (John 18:28). So Pilate, the Roman governor, is the one who has to walk out to them. Think of a guest who won't come past the front mat, so the host ends up holding the whole conversation on the porch.

explanations.answer: So the guards won't turn them away
explanations.explanation: Nobody turns them away in this scene. Not a guard, not a gate. John says they stayed out to avoid being defiled and unable to eat the Passover. They stopped themselves at the door, and Pilate came out to them.

explanations.answer: So the people outside can hear the trial
explanations.explanation: The text gives no such reason. Look at what happens next: when Pilate questions Jesus, he goes back inside the Praetorium and summons Him (John 18:33). The stated reason is about being defiled and unable to eat the Passover. Not one word about a crowd getting a good seat.

explanations.answer: He wouldn't be here if He weren't a criminal
explanations.explanation: Right. They said, "If He were not a criminal, we would not have handed Him over to you." Pilate asked for an accusation and they never named a crime. It's like asking a coworker why the meeting got moved and hearing "because it got moved." Round and round we go.

explanations.answer: He stole money from the temple treasury
explanations.explanation: No theft is mentioned anywhere in this scene. Pilate asks, "What accusation are you bringing against this man?" and they answer, "If He were not a criminal, we would not have handed Him over to you." No money, no treasury, no list of crimes.

explanations.answer: He threatened to burn down the city
explanations.explanation: That charge never comes up here. When Pilate asks for the accusation, the Jews just say, "If He were not a criminal, we would not have handed Him over to you." Nobody names a threat against the city. I'd have remembered a fire threat, baker. That's a big one.
Not quite. Pilate does say, "You take Him and judge Him by your own law…" But the Jews don't take Him. They reply, "We are not permitted to execute anyone…" (John 18:31).

Yes, it's false. Pilate says, "You take Him and judge Him by your own law…" and they push back with, "We are not permitted to execute anyone…" (John 18:31). Nobody walks Jesus back out the door. The matter stays in Pilate's hands.

explanations.answer: Whether He is the King of the Jews
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Pilate goes back in, summons Jesus, and asks, "Are You the King of the Jews?" (John 18:33). He doesn't open with small talk. Straight to the big question, no warm-up.

explanations.answer: Whether He is a prophet from Galilee
explanations.explanation: Pilate never asks that here. His first question is, "Are You the King of the Jews?" Galilee doesn't come up anywhere in this passage. It's a fine question for a different conversation.

explanations.answer: Whether He has an army of followers
explanations.explanation: Pilate doesn't ask about an army. His first words to Jesus inside are, "Are You the King of the Jews?" Jesus does bring up His servants later, when He says they would fight if His kingdom were of this world (John 18:36). But that's Jesus talking, not Pilate asking.
True. Pilate says, "Your own people and chief priests handed You over to me. What have You done?" He starts by asking, "Am I a Jew?" So he's pointing at who brought Jesus to him.
It's actually true. Pilate says, "Your own people and chief priests handed You over to me. What have You done?" That's what he tells Jesus, right after he asks, "Am I a Jew?" (John 18:35).

Yes, world. Jesus says, "My kingdom is not of this world…" He says it again in different words at the end: "…My kingdom is not of this realm." He answers Pilate's question about a kingdom by telling him where His kingdom is not from.

Fight is right. Jesus says, "if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest by the Jews." That tells us something about the kind of kingdom this is. His servants aren't swinging for Him in this room.
Jesus doesn't say city. He says, "My kingdom is not of this world…" (John 18:36). Then He adds, "…My kingdom is not of this realm."
Plead isn't the word. Jesus says His servants would fight to prevent His arrest. That's a different picture than pleading, and the text only uses fight.
Pray isn't in this verse. Jesus says, "if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest by the Jews." The word is fight. Then He adds, "…My kingdom is not of this realm."

explanations.answer: Everyone who belongs to the truth
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Jesus says, "Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice." That comes right after He says He was born and came into the world to testify to the truth. It's a kingdom with a different kind of door.

explanations.answer: Everyone who belongs to the temple
explanations.explanation: The temple isn't mentioned here. Jesus says, "Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice." He's talking to Pilate, and the temple never comes up in that conversation.
Jesus doesn't say Israel here. His words are, "Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice." He's answering a Roman governor, and He ties listening to the truth, not to a nation.
True. Pilate goes out and tells them, "I find no basis for a charge against Him." That's the first time he says it. It won't be the last, baker.
It's true, actually. After his talk with Jesus, Pilate goes out again to the Jews and tells them, "I find no basis for a charge against Him." (John 18:38). He says it plainly. Nothing sneaky in it.
That's him. "Not this man…" they shouted, "but Barabbas!" John adds, "(Now Barabbas was an insurrectionist.)" Pilate offered them a choice and they picked someone else.
That name doesn't show up in this scene. The crowd shouts, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" And John adds that Barabbas was an insurrectionist. Easy one to mix up in a crowd of names.
That name isn't in this scene either. They shout, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" John tells us one more thing about him: he was an insurrectionist. That's the name to hold onto.
Purple it is. John says the soldiers "…dressed Him in a purple robe." (John 19:2). They twisted a crown of thorns and set it on His head too. I'll say only that this is a heavy part of the story.
John doesn't say white. The soldiers dressed Him in a purple robe, and they set a crown of thorns on His head. I think this is a heavy moment, baker.
Brown isn't the color. John says the soldiers "…dressed Him in a purple robe." It's a heavy verse, baker, and the text is plain about it.

Yes. "As soon as the chief priests and officers saw Him, they shouted, 'Crucify Him! Crucify Him!'" It's right when they see Him. There's no waiting around. Pilate answers them, "You take Him and crucify Him…" (John 19:6).
They don't shout that. John says they shouted, "Crucify Him! Crucify Him!" Pilate answers them with, "You take Him and crucify Him…" The word on the table is crucify.
No one says that here. When the chief priests and officers see Him, they shout, "Crucify Him! Crucify Him!" Herod isn't named anywhere in this passage.

explanations.answer: He declared Himself the Son of God
explanations.explanation: That's their reason. They say, "We have a law, and according to that law He must die, because He declared Himself to be the Son of God." And when Pilate hears it, he is even more afraid (John 19:8).

explanations.answer: He healed people on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Not in this passage. The reason they give here is that He "…declared Himself to be the Son of God." Nothing about healing or the Sabbath comes up in this scene.
That isn't what they say here. Their reason is, "…because He declared Himself to be the Son of God." And Pilate's reaction is that he becomes even more afraid.
No, He doesn't. Pilate asks, "Where are You from?" and John says, "But Jesus gave no answer." So the question just hangs there.
That's right. Pilate asks, "Where are You from?" and the text says, "But Jesus gave no answer." It's quiet in that room. Pilate is left with his own question.
That's what Jesus says: "You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above." Pilate had just listed his own authority. Jesus answers by telling him where it comes from.

Jesus doesn't say Caesar, the Roman emperor. He says, "You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above." Caesar does come up in this scene, but it's the crowd who brings him up, not Jesus.

explanations.answer: It is given by the people
explanations.explanation: That isn't what Jesus says. His words are, "You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above." The word is above, not the people.

explanations.answer: The one who handed Him over to Pilate
explanations.explanation: Right. Jesus says, "Therefore the one who handed Me over to you is guilty of greater sin." He says "to you," so He isn't pointing at Pilate. The text doesn't name who He means here.
That's not what Jesus says. His words are, "Therefore the one who handed Me over to you is guilty of greater sin." The soldiers aren't named in that sentence.
Jesus says, "…the one who handed Me over to you…" He's speaking to Pilate, and "to you" means the one doing the handing over is someone else. So the answer isn't the governor himself.

True. The Jews keep shouting, "If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar." They add, "Anyone who declares himself a king is defying Caesar." From then on, that's the pressure sitting on Pilate.

It's true, actually. John says the Jews kept shouting, "If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Anyone who declares himself a king is defying Caesar." (John 19:12). That's right after Pilate begins trying to release Him.

That's it, baker. Pilate "…sat on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, which in Hebrew is Gabbatha." So he's sitting officially now. John then says it was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour. And Pilate tells the Jews, "Here is your King!" (John 19:13-14).
No ivory in this verse. John says Pilate sat on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement. A fancy throne would be a bigger story, but the text doesn't give us one.
Moses' seat isn't mentioned here. John says Pilate sat on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement. It's the seat of a Roman governor, and that's all the text says.

explanations.answer: We have no king but Caesar
explanations.explanation: That's what the chief priests say. After Pilate asks, "Shall I crucify your King?" they answer, "We have no king but Caesar…" It's a short, flat answer, and then Pilate hands Jesus over (John 19:16).

explanations.answer: Our only King is the Lord
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. The chief priests answer, "We have no king but Caesar…" Those are the words John records.
They don't say that here. Earlier, Pilate had told them, "You take Him and crucify Him…" (John 19:6). But when he asks, "Shall I crucify your King?" their answer is, "We have no king but Caesar…"

No, he doesn't. Pilate had said more than once that he found no basis for a charge. Even so, John says, "Then Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers took Him away." He doesn't set Him free.

That's right. Pilate said he found no basis for a charge against Him (John 19:4). He says it again in John 19:6: "I find no basis for a charge against Him." Still, "…Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers took Him away." It's a hard place to stop, baker, and this story isn't over.
